content: The Ministry of Health, the Departmental Service (La Paz Headquarters), the National Service of Agricultural Health and Food Safety, and the Vice Ministry of Rural Development and Lands were represented by individuals such as Fernando Abad Lanza Amuzquibar, Álvaro Argandoña, Freddy Armijo, Marcelo Melean Callisaya Quispe, Erasmo Cordero López, Kelly Natalia Laura Cuellar, Maya Espinoza, Lilian Flores Sermiños, Daniel Gareca Vaca, Liliana Justiniano, Ramiro Omar Mamani, Alcides Medina Pacheco, Miguel Ángel Quispe Gonza, Grover Paredes, and Marín Ruiz Daza. Delegates from the Pan American Health Organization (PAHO) included Meritxell Donadeu, Percy Halkyer, Ana Lucíañez, Baldomero Molina Flores, Marco Antonio Natal Vigilato, Maria Nazario, Rubén Santiago Nicholls, and Alfonso Tenorio. In September 2022, a meeting was held with representatives from the Peruvian Ministry of Health at the national level and from departments with endemicity, as well as representatives from the Ministry of Health’s Strategy on Zoonoses and the Directorate of Animal Health. Participants included Isidro Antitupa Janampa, Román Bances Santamaria, Rubén Bascopé Quispe, Henry Blanco, José Bustamante Navarro, Héctor Castañeda Besares, Luis Arturo Estares Porras, Ana Cecilia Fernández, Ubaldo Flores Barrueta, Arturo Giraldo, Nelly Nidia Huamani Basilio de Cisneros, Yohana Julca Calle, Angela Laos Bejarano, Antonio Loarte Ortega, Jorge Mantilla Salazar, Ynes Monroy Talavera, Ana María Navarro Vela, Luis Oliva Cerna, Martim Ortiz Morera, Karim Pardo, Andrea Pariona Diaz, Jorge Pastor Miranda, Yolanda Pérez Nieto, William Quispe Paredes, Jesús Rodríguez Chávez, Elizabeth Sánchez, Verónica Soto Calle, Kathia Tarqui Terrones, Angélica Terashima Iwashita, Elena Varga Linares, Nathaly Velarde Warthon, Santiago Mauricio Ventocilla, and Rubén Villacqui Ayllon. PAHO delegates at this meeting included Meritxell Donadeu, Ana Lucíañez, Baldomero Molina Flores, Marco Antonio Natal Vigilato, Maria Nazario, Rubén Santiago Nicholls, Hans Salas, and Maria Ester Salazar. In May 2023, an expert meeting was held with participants such as Annia Alba Menéndez from the Department of Parasitology at the Pedro Kourí Institute of Tropical Medicine in Cuba; René Angles Riveros from the Faculty of Medicine at Universidad Mayor de San Andrés in La Paz, Bolivia; Rolando Ayaqui Flores from the Faculty of Medicine at the National University of San Agustín in Arequipa, Peru; María Dolores Bargues from the Department of Parasitology at the Faculty of Pharmacy, University of Valencia, Spain; Miguel M. Cabada from the Institute of Tropical Medicine at Universidad Peruana Cayetano Heredia and the Infectious Diseases Division at the University of Texas, representing both Peru and the United States; Omar dos Santos Carvalho from the René Rachou Institute at the Oswaldo Cruz Foundation in Brazil; Santiago Mas Coma from the WHO Collaborating Center on Fascioliasis and its Snail Vectors in Spain; Marcelo Molento from the Department of Veterinary Medicine at the Federal University of Paraná in Brazil; and Iván Darío Vélez Bernal from the Program for the Study and Control of Tropical Diseases at the University of Antioquia in Colombia. Organizers from PAHO/WHO included Albis Gabrielli from WHO in Switzerland, Ana Lucíañez from PAHO in the United States, Baldomero Molina Flores from PANAFTOSA in Brazil, Santiago Nicholls from PAHO in the United States, and Meritxell Donadeu, a PAHO consultant from Australia. In June 2023, a meeting was held with representatives from Bolivia and Peru. Bolivian participants included delegates from the Ministry of Health, the Departmental Service (La Paz Headquarters), the National Service of Agricultural Health and Food Safety, and the Vice Ministry of Rural Development and Lands. Representatives included Dina Condori, Erasmo Cordero, Carla Espinoza, Miguel Angel Estrada, Daniel Gareca, Alfredo Laime, Fernando Lanza, Blas Mamani, Pedro Medina, Oscar Mendoza, Grover Paredes, Elizardo Peralta, and Lily Susana. Peruvian participants included delegates from the Ministry of Health (national level) and from departments with endemicity, as well as representatives from the Ministry of Health’s Health Strategy on Zoonoses and the Directorate of Animal Health. Participants included Isidro Antitupa Janampa, Román Bances Santa María, Rubén Bascopé Quispe, José Luis Bustamante Navarro, Eric Callapiña Enriquez, Cesar Augusto Canales Santillán, Olimpia Chuquista Alcarraz, Dante de la Vega Cavero, Luis Arturo Estares Porras, Ubaldo Flores Barrueta, Ángel Gómez Marín, Yonny Gonzales Almonacid, Hector Guevara Pineda, Luis Miguel Huaman Ticona, Naum Huicho Yanasupo, Marco Marino Mercado Apaza, Rodolfo Miranda Obando, William Quispe Paredes, Jesús Rodríguez Chávez, Raymundo Rojas Neyra, Robinson Rojas Rivera, Brizeida Valdez Castillo, Nury Vargas Mayuri, and Nathaly Velarde Warthon. PAHO delegates at this meeting included Patricia Chávez, Meritxell Donadeu, Percy Halkyer, Ana Lucíañez, Baldomero Molina Flores, Rubén Santiago Nicholls, Maria Esther Salazar, and María Jesús Sánchez. Fascioliasis is a parasitic disease that affects humans and a wide range of animals, primarily herbivores. In Latin America and the Caribbean, it is caused by the trematode Fasciola hepatica. The World Health Organization (WHO) classifies fascioliasis as a neglected tropical disease. The Pan American Health Organization (PAHO), as part of its commitment to the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development and the Sustainable Health Agenda for the Americas 2018–2030, has launched an initiative to eliminate communicable diseases in the Americas. One of its objectives is to eliminate fascioliasis as a public health problem in the region by 2030. Operational guidelines have been developed to provide information and guidance to endemic countries to help achieve this goal. These guidelines were prepared with the support of technical staff and expert professionals from the region and the WHO Collaborating Center on fascioliasis and its snail vectors. They incorporate current practices and consider the challenges and specific characteristics of endemic areas. While fascioliasis in animals causes economic losses in many countries, human fascioliasis is limited to environments with the ethnographic characteristics and socioeconomic determinants necessary for human infection. These operational guidelines focus on these areas, which are generally associated with small farmers and rural communities. They are part of the “One Health” approach, integrating different sectors and working in synergy to make interventions more effective and sustainable.
